title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI systems were used to create a fabricated interview between real public figures that never occurred, then deployed in a fake article designed to drive investment in an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The system generated convincing false content at scale, relying on the authority of the impersonated figures and polished presentation to bypass investor skepticism. Catching this would have required verification that the interview actually took place, either through the broadcasters involved or through checking the credentials of the platform being promoted.

This is a deployment of AI for impersonation and fraud. The scam exploited the difficulty of distinguishing AI-generated false content from legitimate reporting, particularly when it borrowed the names and likenesses of trusted figures. It was not a model making a factual error in good faith, but a system deliberately misused to create deceptive material.

It is not established who created the fake content, what specific AI tools were used, or how many people were defrauded by this particular article.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article recently circulated featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in an interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler. The fabricated story described an increasingly heated exchange about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn against. The interview never actually occurred, representing a growing trend of AI-generated scams that create convincing false content to defraud investors.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports this type of scam is becoming more prevalent and sophisticated. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams overall, with phishing scams jumping 279 percent and fake investment platforms increasing 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated figure, followed by politicians and business leaders like Alan Kohler, who has been targeted multiple times. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
